fufu was written for one working tree. Every per-repository assumption in it — one operation log, one undo pointer, one lock, one ref table — was correct for exactly as long as a repository had exactly one checkout, and wrong the moment it had two. That is not a rare shape: a pool of worktrees is how several agents work at once, and it is the shape fufu is built to make survivable. This release is that whole seam, plus the three surfaces a fleet needs to be legible from outside — a sideways axis between branches, a stream of the log, and a way for another program to be a fufu verb.

**The corruption, first**

`ff undo` in the main worktree moved HEAD to a linked worktree's branch, overwrote the main worktree's files with that worktree's, and left both trees standing on one branch — a state git itself refuses to create. Reading in a linked worktree appended a foreign operation to the shared chain just by looking. This was reproducible, and it is what the first half of the release exists to close.

The log was always worktree-scoped; with one worktree the repository and the worktree were the same object and the ref name said so. It lives at `refs/fufu/wt/<id>/ops` now, with `refs/fufu/wt/<id>/trash/@ops` beside it, where `<id>` is the worktree's gitdir basename — `main` for the main worktree — which git keeps stable across `git worktree move` and rebuilds on `git worktree repair`. A worktree's chain is parentless: rooting it in another tree's would present that tree's operations as this one's past and entangle trim across trees.

The chain stays in the shared ref namespace rather than moving under `refs/worktree/`, and that is a measured constraint rather than a preference. On git 2.50.1, `git gc` from the main worktree collects objects pinned only by a linked worktree's `refs/worktree/*` ref, while a shared `refs/fufu/*` ref survives the same run. Reachability is the whole of fufu's gc pin, so a per-worktree namespace would silently lose captures. That same fact is what lets a chain outlive the worktree it belonged to, which is what the agent-deleted-my-bay case needs.

Everything downstream follows from the split. The lock moves to `<common-dir>/fufu/oplog-<id>`, so two worktrees stop serializing against each other for no correctness gain. The id index is one file per chain with resolution reading the union, keeping one global id space and no cross-worktree invalidation on the read path. Migration runs at the top of both reconcile and capture, before either reads a tip, and carries the reflog by replay — undo's forward scan reads it, and losing it loses redo. Both names holding a chain is reported rather than resolved: fufu does not silently destroy history, even where it is being abandoned.

An operation records the state of the world it left behind, and `ff undo` moves every ref where that table and the observed present disagree. The table was repository-wide, which is why one tree's undo reverted another tree's branch. A worktree now records only the refs it owns — `refs/heads/<b>` and `refs/fufu/parked/<b>` are dropped where `<b>` is checked out elsewhere, while tags stay and so does `refs/stash`, verified as one stack shared by every worktree and therefore nobody's exclusively. The narrowing is on the table and not on the diff, because CAS expectations come from the observed present and a crash mid-move has to see the remainder as the new diff.

And a second worktree's first command stopped being read as a first run. `park_legacy` fires when the log is absent and moves everything under `refs/fufu/snap/` aside as pre-cutover wreckage — sound when "no log" could only mean fufu had never run here, and false once it means "no log for this worktree". A new bay's very first command in a repository fufu had been writing for months orphaned every other worktree's branch pointer into `refs/fufu/legacy/`. A chain existing anywhere in the repository now means the cutover is behind us.

**A branch is only ever open in one worktree**

git refuses to check out a branch two worktrees already hold. fufu moves HEAD through a gix ref transaction with `PreviousValue::Any`, which enforces nothing, so `ff switch side` from the main worktree succeeded while a bay stood on `side`.

The guard that raised the right error existed and nothing called it on the path that opens a branch — and it carried two bugs of its own. It enumerated `repo.worktrees()`, which is linked-only by gix's own definition, so a linked worktree could never learn that the *main* worktree held a branch: it worked in one direction, and the direction it missed is the common one. And it did not exclude itself, so a linked worktree renaming its own branch tripped over its own HEAD. Both are answered by one reader that enumerates the linked worktrees and the main one and skips the tree it is running in. The call sits in `switch`, which covers `ff switch`, `ff start`, `ff edit` and the `ff switch <rev>` redirect, after the same-branch early return and before the not-found raise. The message is git's, naming the branch and the path.

`ff restack` moves the branch you named and no other. A rewrite re-parents a range and then moved every local head whose tip landed inside it, so restacking one branch silently carried its descendants and siblings — including a branch another worktree was standing on, whose index and tree then disagreed with its own HEAD. Everything the rewrite map touched other than the named branch is now left where it stood and named in the output, warning-painted. The narrowing is at the restack call site and not in the rewrite: `ff reword`, `ff absorb`, `ff lift` and `ff done` all need the carried set, and narrowing it at the source would have stopped four verbs from moving branches they are supposed to move with nothing failing to say so. This deliberately diverges from `git rebase --update-refs`, which carries every ref in the range — git's rebase assumes exclusive control of the one worktree doing it, and fufu cannot.

**`ff worktree`**

`ff worktree add <path> [<branch>]`, `ff worktree list`, `ff worktree remove <path-or-id>`.

gix has no worktree-creation API, so fufu lays git's on-disk layout itself, byte for byte, read off a live linked worktree rather than inferred. The checkout needs no new dependency: writing the index for a tree and applying a transition from the empty tree makes every path an addition, which is what a checkout is. The new worktree is opened by finding its proxy rather than by discovering from its path, so a successful open is proof the layout is well-formed — and the checkout goes through *that* handle, never the caller's, since writing another tree's branch through the calling worktree is the corruption the rest of this release exists to fix.

Both directions are real operations. A creation lays the new worktree's chain floor as it goes, so `ff undo` works in the bay from its first command rather than its second — that chain existing before you have typed anything there is the whole difference from `git worktree add`. A removal captures the tree first, into that tree's own chain, under that chain's lock, and that is why the verb has no `--force`: git demands one for a dirty worktree because it has nowhere to put the work, and fufu put it somewhere a line earlier. The removal moves no ref on purpose, so the chain survives and the capture stays addressable after the checkout is gone.

Which is what makes the listing's second section worth having. `git worktree list` cannot know about it: after the live worktrees, `ff worktree list` prints the operation chains whose worktree is gone, each row an address rather than a memorial — the tip is an operation id in the same twelve-letter prefix `ff op log` uses, and `ff restore <path> --at-op <op>` takes it directly. Someone whose agent deleted a bay finds the id there and pulls the file back through verbs that already existed.

`ff undo` reverses a worktree in both directions. Leaving an add retires the worktree — capturing into its own chain and then tearing it down, which is what makes an undo allowed to delete a directory — and entering one revives it, resolving what to check out from the capture the effect names, then the chain's own tip, then the branch. The middle step is why undoing an add and redoing it returns the uncommitted work rather than a clean tree. The worktree comes back under its original id, because the chain is keyed by it. The worktree step runs first in the effect loop, ahead of the stash and the refs, because it holds the only refusal in the move: a worktree with a fufu command running in it cannot be captured, and a move that cannot capture must not destroy.

Under `fufu.translate`, `git worktree add <path>` and `git worktree add <path> <branch>` now find the fufu verb. Nothing else about `worktree` translates — and `remove` deliberately falls through to git verbatim, because fufu's removal captures the tree first and a translation that silently did more than the command asked would be the wrong kind of helpful.

Retention caught up too. The auto-trim stamp is per chain rather than per repository, so one `ff status` in one worktree no longer consumes the daily budget for all of them and then trims only its own. And a removed worktree's chain had nobody to trim it: `ff trim` is now a driver that does this worktree's chain and then every orphan — a chain whose worktree is gone — leaving another *live* worktree's chain alone, since it has a process of its own and its lock is not this pass's to wait on. Only this worktree's pass earns the trim note, because appending onto a dead tree's chain from a process that does not own it would be writing history in someone else's name.

**`ff collide` — the sideways axis**

fufu measured a branch on two axes and both pointed vertically: the base beneath it, and the remote copy of itself. Neither answers the question two people working at once actually have — would this branch and that one collide?

`ff collide [<branch>...]` prints one line per pair, with the paths where two branches touch the same thing, and closes with the largest set that touches nothing. The engine is one three-way merge per pair from the merge base, so there is no commit walk, no depth cap, and the only unknown left is two histories with no base at all. A collision is an undirected edge, so there is no order to sort into — if two branches collide, no sequence saves them — and what a caller wants is the clear set, picked greedily newest-first, called greedy on the field because the exact answer is NP-hard and a set that claims to be best without saying how is a set nobody should trust. An unknown blocks admission exactly as a collision does.

What earns the verb is the tree each side is measured by: the branch's open change, read from the operation log rather than from a worktree. A branch checked out somewhere else — or nowhere — still answers, and a name wears a `*` when it has work that has not been committed. Two people editing the same lines are visible to each other before either has committed anything, which is the half of the day every tracker built on commits is blind to.

The glyph carries the verdict and the color only repeats it — `✓` clear, `✕` collides, `?` can't say — so a monochrome terminal loses decoration and never information. Fewer than two branches is a state and not a failure, and neither is a collision: this verb reports, and reporting a finding is not failing.

**`ff watch` — the log gets subscribers**

The log is already an event log; `ff watch` is the verb that lets something else read it as one. Status lines, editor plugins, dashboards and agent supervisors get newline-delimited JSON, one object per motion, instead of polling `ff log --json` in a loop. It is not a daemon: a foreground process you started, holding no authority, writing nothing.

A subscriber is not told what was *appended*, because the append-only model is wrong in every direction the log actually moves. An undo steps the pointer backwards and writes onto the side it abandons; `ff op restore` across a fork lands on an id that is neither ancestor nor descendant; new work after an undo is a sibling; a trim replays what survives and rewrites every surviving id, so the address space a subscriber holds stops resolving. `Start`, `Landed`, `SteppedBack`, `Forked`, `Rewritten` is the closed set of honest answers, and every walk follows the `fufu-prev` trailer rather than the commit graph — an operation's second parent is a real commit from your history, and a graph walk wanders straight out of the log and into it.

`--all` is one process over every chain in the repository, and the `worktree` field rides every line in both modes. It is an added field, so the contract stays at 1 and anything parsing today keeps working. The `--all` loop ticks before it sleeps, because its first tick is the anchor burst; the single-tree loop sleeps first, so a `--since` replay cannot race the anchor read that just settled. A rewrite is terminal per chain rather than per stream: it is emitted for its chain, that chain re-anchors, and the stream continues — so the exit-1 rewrite contract stays the single-tree one. The chain set only grows: a chain not seen before is anchored and announced, which collapses the first tick and a later `ff worktree add` into one path, and a retired chain stays, because `ff worktree remove` captures into it before the directory goes and dropping it at a tick boundary would race the last thing it ever said.

`--since` replays from an anchor before tailing, `--kind` and `--session` filter through the core's own vocabulary, `-n` stops after a count, and `fufu.watchInterval` sets the poll at 200ms with a 10ms floor — a tick is two ref lookups against a held packed-refs buffer, so it is sub-millisecond work five times a second, and a knob that lets a foreground process spin a core is a knob with a bug in it. `--all` with `--since` is refused: an operation belongs to one chain, so there is no single place for a repository-wide stream to replay from.

**An extension is a binary**

`ff tower next --peek` finds an executable named `ff-tower` on PATH and hands it `next --peek`, the way git has always found `git-lfs`. There is no plugin API, no registry, and nothing to install into fufu — a name and a directory on PATH is the whole contract, which is what makes it something a program in another language, or another repository, can satisfy.

Parse first, PATH second, and that ordering is the design: the dispatch is reached only from clap's unknown-subcommand path, so a builtin always wins without a rule saying it does. Put an `ff-status` on PATH and `ff status` is still fufu's, and a word that resolves nowhere gets clap's own error back verbatim, `ff stauts` still suggesting `status`. The name is validated before anything touches the filesystem, and that is a security check rather than a tidiness one: it arrives from a command line, and `ff ../../evil` would otherwise build a path that walks out of the PATH directory it was joined to.

The child inherits three variables: `FF_REPO`, the worktree fufu was invoked against, unset rather than empty outside one; `FF_CONTRACT`, the integer every `{"ff": 1, …}` envelope carries; and `FF_SESSION`, which is what lets one `ff undo` step over a whole flight's captures rather than one keystroke of them. `FF_REPO` is emitted and never read back — fufu answers which repository from the current directory alone, so a stale export cannot silently redirect a later call the way `GIT_DIR` can. Capture runs first and loudly, exactly as `ff git` does, and everything after the extension's word passes through untouched, `--json` included: once dispatch happens the stream belongs to the extension.

`ff -C <dir>` (`--cwd`) is git's spelling of the missing flag, and the mechanism is a chdir before anything discovers, so all forty-three discovery sites are correct with no threading and a relative path argument after it resolves against `<dir>` too. It runs before the pre-command capture, so that capture is taken in the repository you named. Any directory inside the repository will do, a linked worktree included, which is how you ask one bay a question without leaving another. A directory that is not there raises `usage/no-such-directory` and captures nothing. It works on the extension dispatch path too, which clap never reaches, so the flag is scanned by hand there in all five spellings.

The `tower` sketch that motivated most of this now lives at [tyler-johnson/tower](https://github.com/tyler-johnson/tower) rather than in a directory under `crates/` that was not a crate. The seam it needs was never fufu's to hold and is already shipped: it spawns `ff <verb> --json` and reads the envelope against `FF_CONTRACT`.

**Smaller things**

The pager scrolls again. `ff log` and its family set `LESS=FRX` when the variable is unset, mirroring git, and the `X` is why the mouse wheel did nothing: `-X` suppresses the terminal init string, less never enters the alternate screen, and a terminal only routes wheel events to a program that is on it. git carries `-X` for a reason that expired in 2018, when less 530 stopped wiping one-screen output under `-F`. Measured here on less 668 under a pty: with four lines, `FR` and `FRX` emit byte-identical output; with 200 lines, `FR` enters the alt screen and `FRX` does not, which is the only case where scrolling was ever wanted. The cost is that long output no longer stays on screen after `q`, which is the trade every pager that scrolls makes.

`ff worktree` was green on Linux and broken on the other two platforms, and CI caught it on the first run to cover either worktree landing. On Windows, `canonicalize` returns an extended-length path, and that prefix went into the admin files git reads, into the operation record, and into `--json` — so git could not parse the worktree it was pointed at and no path fufu printed was one a person could type. Stripping the prefix was not enough: git finds a worktree's directory by stripping `/.git` off the end of its `gitdir` file, and a path spelled with backslashes does not end in `/.git`, so the strip failed silently. On macOS the temporary directory is reached through a symlink, so the path fufu recorded and the path a person types differ by a `/private` nobody typed, and `ff worktree remove <path>` compared the two with `==`. One module decides all of it now — what fufu records and prints, what the files git reads back are written as, and whether two spellings name the same worktree — so a message, a listing and a JSON row can no longer disagree about a path. The differential test that should have caught the Windows failure had passed on the broken output, because `…/bay/.git` contains `…/bay`: it now reads `git worktree list --porcelain` and compares whole fields.

**Numbers**

32 commits over v0.7.0, +8,026/−661 across 78 files. 1,364 workspace tests, up from 1,252. 108 `ff explain` ids, up from 101. Three new verbs — `ff collide`, `ff watch`, `ff worktree` — plus PATH dispatch for `ff <name>`, and one new global flag.

Every claim above was re-checked against the built binary rather than the commit bodies that introduced it: a bay made and listed with git agreeing about its branch and git dir, `ff switch` refused in both directions with git's own message, `ff restack` naming the descendant it left behind while git's `--update-refs` would have moved it, `ff worktree remove` printing the capture id and `ff restore --at-op` pulling an uncommitted file back out of a chain whose checkout is gone, `ff undo` reviving that bay under its original id with its uncommitted work intact, two branches colliding over work neither has committed, `ff watch --all` opening with one anchor line per worktree and refusing `--since`, an `ff-probe` on PATH receiving argv, `FF_REPO`, `FF_CONTRACT` and `FF_SESSION` while a builtin refused to be shadowed, `ff -C` reaching into a bay from outside it, `ff trim` naming the dead bay it aged out, and `git worktree add` translating while `git worktree remove` falls through.
